title: Ajahn Funn: Having heard this, then opanayiko – bring it inside and look within. Do people die and then get reborn? Look at ourselves: are…
content:
Washing Away Kamma by Sitting in Samādhi Until the Mind Is Peaceful

Having heard this, then opanayiko – bring it inside and look within. Do people die and then get reborn? Look at ourselves: are we being reborn right now? Are we doing it right now? Is our mind staying still? Come on, bring the opanayika dhamma and look inside. Can our mind stay still? It is producing bhava and jāti – who knows how many bhava? It concocts, it fabricates, it produces there, it ceases here, produces there. It goes on like that. How many bhava has it been? Right now as we sit here, this birth – we cannot prevent it. That is why the Buddha taught us to contemplate buddho.

At the same time, he taught us to contemplate these devadūta, bring them up within our own mind. Suffering, which is this birth, we must stop it. Wash away demerit and kamma, cut off demerit and kamma. We cannot wash it away with a knife or a sword, nor with water. Only by sitting in samādhi until the mind is peaceful. When the mind is peaceful, it is empty, nothing at all. There is only lightness and ease, cool body and cool mind, ending suffering and difficulty, ending trouble and vexation. Only buddho, the joy; buddho, the brightness; buddho, the clarity. All kamma ends, all evil ends. Only buddho, the joy. Therefore, our refuge must depend on this knowledge.

title: Ajahn Funn: What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? When the mind is in the sensual plane, it roams among…
content:
Transcending the Sensual Plane: Contemplating the Body to Generate Disenchantment

What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? When the mind is in the sensual plane, it roams among forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental phenomena (dhammārammaṇa) – that is its object. It is called one who delights in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, contacts, and various mental objects. This is called the mind abiding in the sensual-sphere realm (kāmāvacara bhūmi), in the existence called the sensual realm (kāmabhava).

What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? It lets go of external forms, external sounds, external smells, external tastes, and the many contacts and mental objects. It sees only this individual body of ours. It contemplates this conditioned body of ours, fixed right on itself, not sending the mind elsewhere or far away. It sees only our own conditioned body – its deterioration, its decay, or sees the conditioned body exactly as it is: with hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin. There is nothing else beyond this, nothing superior to this. Whether happiness or suffering, seeing deterioration and decay, or seeing breaking apart, the mind then abandons this form. Nibbidā arises – disenchantment with this form. Because this form has no core, no substance, no essence.

title: Ajahn Funn: When we were monks, we had many trainings and many duties. Just the thirteen dhutaṅga (ascetic practices) alone were there. Now that we…
content:
Three Duties of a Lay Practitioner: Dāna, Sīla, Bhāvanā

When we were monks, we had many trainings and many duties. Just the thirteen dhutaṅga (ascetic practices) alone were there. Now that we have disrobed and become laymen, we have only three duties: dāna-vatta – the duty of giving offerings and making merit; sīla-vatta – the duty of observing precepts; and bhāvanā-vatta – the duty of meditation. Doing these daily as our regular practice – the things we wish for in this world – are just these three duties.

Our aims: firstly, we want to have lots of material possessions, money, and wealth. Secondly, we want beautiful forms and appearances, long life, freedom from disease and danger. Thirdly, we want wisdom and intelligence. That’s all. So we study and learn. Why doesn’t everyone succeed in achieving their aspirations? It’s because we lack the supporting conditions – we lack the habits, i.e., the actual doing of these things. We are lacking those three duties.

Therefore, we must have confidence in the results (ānisaṃsa) of what we have done through these duties. For example, if we want material possessions, money, and wealth, we must rely on the ānisaṃsa of our own generosity. When we have given gifts and made merit, then in whatever birth or realm we are born in – whether in this life or future lives – that ānisaṃsa will reflect back its results, so we obtain wealth, become one who does not starve or suffer want, one who is not poor or in difficulty. This is because we have already deposited it in the Buddha’s Dispensation, buried it within our own minds, because we have done it, we have built it.

title: Ajahn Funn: Kamma does not arise elsewhere. Right now, our body is not doing anything, our speech is not doing anything. Only mental kamma remains…
content:
All Good and Evil – Mind Is the Foremost

Kamma does not arise elsewhere. Right now, our body is not doing anything, our speech is not doing anything. Only mental kamma remains — the act of inclining. Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayā — all good and evil, mind is the foremost. You should all examine this clearly, with certainty. Good and evil — mind comes first.

Mano means inclining. Dhammā means thoughts. Pubba means "in the beginning." This is the origin of all merit and wholesomeness — our own mind. Good and evil arise from this, not from anywhere far away. Contemplate this firmly, right now.

In the past, when the Buddha taught, the members of his audience, after listening to his exhortations and instructions — the Dhamma, his teachings — attained path and fruit, becoming stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmī), non-returners (anāgāmī), and arahants. These days, we listen but do not gain any substance or meaning. We listen just as a formality, listening only to get merit, not knowing where merit is. When the sermon ends, we say sādhu and think we have gained merit. But where would that merit come from?

title: Ajahn Funn: So listen to your heart. Whatever it’s like, know it right here. Good or bad, examine the merit in your heart. You’ve come…
content:
Sitting in Concentration Once Is Greater Than Giving Donations a Hundred Times

So listen to your heart. Whatever it’s like, know it right here. Good or bad, examine the merit in your heart. You’ve come to make merit, so examine your heart. Just 15 minutes, that’s all. It’s not much. You’ve traveled a great distance and are tired. What other kind of merit can equal this? Giving donations 100 times, 1,000 times, can’t equal sitting in concentration just once. Its rewards are great. So keep making merit, doing what’s good, creating goodness so that our nation will be happy and at peace, in reliance on the Buddha’s teachings.

What did the Buddha teach? He taught our body. He taught our heart to abandon evil. He was afraid we’d be suffering, afraid we’d be in trouble, afraid we’d be destitute, so he taught us to do good through our body, speech, and mind, so that we’d meet with happiness and prosperity.

That’s the Dhamma he taught in his first discourse, Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion. In short, the body and mind are the foundation for the Buddha’s teachings, the foundation for the paths and their fruitions, the foundation for happiness and prosperity.

title: Ajahn Funn: If we abstain from these five faults, the Buddha said: sīlena sugatiṃ yanti – through virtue one goes to a happy destiny. One…
content:
Sīlena Sugatiṃ Yanti: By Virtue One Goes to a Happy Destiny

If we abstain from these five faults, the Buddha said: sīlena sugatiṃ yanti – through virtue one goes to a happy destiny. One has happiness wherever one goes because the five faults are gone. Wherever one stays, one is happy. Sitting, lying, standing, walking are all happy. From now on, abstain from these five things and do not do them. When we abstain, all that kamma ends. If we don’t abstain, it doesn’t end. It becomes karmic accumulation, karmic continuation. The troubles we have now are because of these five faults – we don’t abstain. If we abstain from these five, we are at ease. The country wouldn’t need police, wouldn’t need soldiers, no prisons, no judges. Think about it. Even a red ant or a tiny insect, the Buddha taught not to harm. Even the blood of a mosquito, we shouldn’t take. There would be no petty thieves, no sexual misconduct, no cheating or deceiving, no intoxicated people. Without these five, where would we find any trouble or conflict? There would be none, wouldn’t there? We would be at ease. We gain wealth and happiness because we abstain from these five faults – not because we do other work. The Buddha didn’t say that by trade or business one goes to a happy destiny. He said: sīlena sugatiṃ yanti – one has happiness because of observing precepts. Sīlena bhogasampadā – one has wealth because of observing precepts.

title: Ajahn Funn: Now, when we contemplate these things and see that they are not a person, they are not beautiful, not handsome, not clean or…
content:
If You Don’t Wash Hair for a Month, How Beautiful Is It? Contemplate and Abandon Attachment

Now, when we contemplate these things and see that they are not a person, they are not beautiful, not handsome, not clean or pure, not good or excellent – when we see like that, our mind withdraws the clinging to aggregates, and we can abandon personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Nowadays we hold that these are beautiful things, that they are a person. What beauty? Hair falls into our rice and food – can we eat it? How is it beautiful? We have to wash and groom it every day. How is it beautiful? Try not washing or grooming it for a month or two. Could you go near anyone? Or what do you say? Body hair and nails – we have to pick and clean them constantly. When they fall into our rice and food, we can’t accept it, right? Teeth – we have to brush them every day, clean them every day. If you don’t clean them for a month, try it. How beautiful, how handsome can they be when they are like that? If a tooth falls into your plate of rice, you throw away the whole plate – you can’t accept it. So how can you say it’s good? We must contemplate to see it like that. And skin – we have to wash it with soap every day. If we don’t wash it for a month, try it. Oh, what is it like? How can you call it beautiful? This is the delusion that makes people so confused. If we see things as they truly are, we abandon personality view. Would anyone accept human skin that fell into their rice? Human skin – they’d throw away the whole plate. So we should know and see this.

title: Ajahn Funn: Try to find a way out—so what if it kills you? What’s wrong with finding a way out? What are you still attached…
content:
Try to Die Outside of the Noose: Don’t Tie Yourself Down

Try to find a way out—so what if it kills you? What’s wrong with finding a way out? What are you still attached to? What are you still infatuated with? Try to be more resolute! We come into this world alone and we go alone. So who is it that dies? What leads us back to birth? Be done with it! Develop your goodness. That’s better than dying in a heap of suffering. Better than dying in worries—dying in the noose. Try to die outside of the noose. That’s what’s really good. Don’t tie yourself down.

It all comes from the mind, fabricating the idea that “This is mine, that’s mine, this property’s mine, this money, these possessions are mine, this clothing is mine, these homes are mine, these children and grandchildren are mine”: nothing but “me” and “mine.”

title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha established the teaching right here: the existence of sīla, samādhi, paññā. Sīla is nothing else; it is our own self as…
content:
Sīla Is with Ourselves, Not with the Buddha or the Monks

The Buddha established the teaching right here: the existence of sīla, samādhi, paññā. Sīla is nothing else; it is our own self as sīla. Restraining body, speech, and mind to be proper. Sīla is right here, not elsewhere. Sīla is not with the Buddha, sīla is not with the monks. Sīla is with ourselves. A person who restrains himself properly, doing no wrong great or small, making body, speech, and mind proper, harmless and non-dangerous – when standing, it is sīla; when walking, it is sīla; when sitting or lying down, it is sīla; wherever one goes, it is sīla. If we do not commit the five wrong actions – pāṇātipātā (killing), adinnādānā (stealing), kāmesumicchācārā (sexual misconduct), musāvādā (false speech), surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā (intoxicants) – then wherever we are, it is sīla. In the forest, in the jungle, in the village, in the city, on the roadside – it is sīla.

title: Ajahn Funn: The purpose of our coming here, every one of you, has no other aim. We want happiness, we want progress, we want only…
content:
The Beginning Is Beautiful: Restraining Body, Speech, and Mind Is Sīla

The purpose of our coming here, every one of you, has no other aim. We want happiness, we want progress, we want only virtue and goodness. So what method should we use to attain happiness and ease? The Buddha laid down the religion and his teachings. He taught about giving (dāna), morality (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). These are the principles of Buddhism. All of us want virtue and goodness. This goodness is nothing else: it is goodness through sīla, goodness through samādhi, goodness through paññā. Regarding that beauty, the Pali says: ādikalyāṇaṃ, majjhekalyāṇaṃ, pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ. Kalyāṇa means beauty. The beginning is beautiful, the beginning is lovely — that is one who has sīla. Let us all know what sīla is. What is sīla? It is not the sky or air, not trees or mountains or hills, not the city or country, not huts, halls, sermon halls, ordination halls, or vihāras. Sīla is our own body, speech, and mind. We restrain our body, speech, and mind to make them proper. We do not commit any wrong, great or small, with body or mind. Then, in whatever realm or birth we take, we become a proper person, a beautiful person.
